lesson.title: The Default Strategy: Life as a C3 Plant
lesson.summary: C3 plants fix carbon dioxide directly through the standard Calvin cycle, producing a three-carbon compound as the first stable product, a strategy that works well in most climates but struggles when it gets hot and dry.
lesson.body:
Every plant discussed so far in this unit, one that fixes carbon dioxide directly using RuBisCO to attach it to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate and produce the three-carbon compound 3-phosphoglycerate as the first stable product, falls into a category called C3 plants, named for that three-carbon molecule. This is the ancestral, default form of photosynthesis, and it remains by far the most common strategy among plant species today, used by the great majority of them, including staple crops like wheat, rice, and soybeans, along with most trees and grasses in temperate climates.

The C3 strategy is straightforward and, under moderate conditions, efficient: carbon dioxide diffuses in through small pores in the leaf called stomata, dissolves into the moist tissue inside the leaf, and is fixed directly by RuBisCO in the mesophyll cells where the Calvin cycle runs. No extra chemical steps, no shuttling molecules between cell types, and no extra ATP cost beyond what the Calvin cycle itself already requires. For a plant growing in a cool, well-watered environment with moderate sunlight, this simplicity is an advantage rather than a weakness.

The trouble starts with the same pores that let carbon dioxide in. Stomata are also the main route through which water vapor escapes a leaf, so on a hot, dry day a plant faces a genuine conflict: keep stomata open to keep fixing carbon and lose water rapidly to the air, or close stomata to conserve water and cut off the carbon dioxide supply. Most C3 plants respond to heat and drought stress by closing their stomata, which is the right call for surviving dehydration but creates an internal problem, since the Calvin cycle keeps consuming whatever carbon dioxide is left inside the leaf while the light reactions keep producing oxygen, so the ratio of oxygen to carbon dioxide inside the leaf's air spaces climbs.

That shift in ratio matters enormously because of RuBisCO's imperfect ability to distinguish carbon dioxide from oxygen at its active site. As internal oxygen rises relative to carbon dioxide, RuBisCO increasingly grabs oxygen instead, triggering the wasteful oxygenase pathway rather than productive carbon fixation. This is the central vulnerability of the C3 strategy, and it is severe enough that on hot, sunny days C3 plants can lose a substantial share of their potential sugar production to this side reaction, which the next chapter examines directly.

This vulnerability is not a flaw that evolution somehow failed to fix in every lineage. In cooler or more humid environments, the tradeoff rarely bites hard enough to matter, which is exactly why C3 photosynthesis remains dominant worldwide. It is only in hot, bright, water-limited habitats that the pressure to solve this problem became strong enough to favor the more elaborate carbon-concentrating strategies that some plant lineages evolved independently, strategies covered later in this unit.
